name: MemAgent

paper.title: MemAgent: Reshaping Long-Context LLM with Multi-Conv RL-based Memory Agent

construction.unit: one free-text memory of at most 1,024 tokens per question
construction.kept_as: LLM-written notes (copied sentences plus the model's comments), rewritten whole after every chunk
construction.processing: the model reads question + previous memory + next 5,000-token chunk and writes a new memory that replaces the old one
construction.writer: RL-trained Qwen2.5-7B/14B-Instruct (RL-MemoryAgent), same model that answers

organization.structure: single text buffer inside the prompt
organization.stores: one memory string; no external store

management.operations: overwrite the whole memory after each chunk
management.conflicts: left to the model; no explicit rule
management.forgetting: implicit: whatever the new memory omits is gone; output beyond 1,024 tokens is cut

retrieval.query: the question is in every update prompt, so writing is question-conditioned
retrieval.candidates: no retrieval: every chunk is read once, in order
retrieval.selection: the RL-trained model decides what to keep while writing
retrieval.budget: memory 1,024 + chunk 5,000 + question 1,024 + output 1,024 tokens (8K window)

use.reasoning: single answer call after K memory updates

classify.note: No store or search: the model streams the whole document and keeps one overwritten text memory; selection happens at write time by an RL-trained policy.

stages.ingestion: The document is tokenised and cut into consecutive 5,000-token chunks that are fed one per call; nothing is indexed.
stages.construction: At each chunk the model sees the question, the previous memory and the chunk, and generates a new memory (at most 1,024 tokens) through a fixed prompt.
stages.update: The new memory overwrites the old one, so keeping, merging and dropping are all implicit in what the model writes.
stages.answer: After the last chunk a second prompt gives the model only the question and the final memory and asks for the answer.
stages.learning: Multi-conv DAPO: all K update calls and the answer call of a rollout share one advantage computed from a rule-based exact-match reward on the final answer (group size 16), in two curriculum stages on synthetic HotpotQA and DocQA data.

summary: An LLM reads a long document chunk by chunk and overwrites a fixed 1,024-token text memory after each chunk; RL on the final answer (Multi-conv DAPO) teaches it what to keep, so an 8K-window model is tested up to 3.5M tokens.
notes:

sources.code_note: Latest commit (2026-05-12, a README change). The evaluation loop (taskutils/memory_eval) and the training agent (recurrent/impls/memory.py) were last changed in July 2025, after paper v1; whether they are exactly the runs behind v2's tables is not stated. The repo has no evaluation code for LongBench-QA/SUM and no stage II training script.

headline: The only memory is one text string of at most 1,024 tokens that the model rewrites after every 5,000-token chunk; the answer call sees only this string and the question.
Nothing is retrieved or revisited: a 3.5M-token input means about 700 update calls in sequence.
What to keep is learned end to end: every update call gets the reward of the final answer (Multi-conv DAPO).

units.role: the whole working state carried from chunk to chunk
units.made_by: the RL-trained model, one update call per chunk

answer_context.sees: the question and one memory of at most 1,024 tokens

compression.what: answer context vs the longest RULER-HQA input

paper_vs_code.paper: Table 5 asks for the answer in \boxed{}
paper_vs_code.code: evaluation uses a template asking for 'Therefore, the answer is ...' (App. A.4 describes this one); \boxed{} is the training template

paper_vs_code.paper: App. A.3: 50 to 6,400 wiki items give about 7K to 3.5M tokens
paper_vs_code.code: 6,400 items is the 896K test; 1.75M and 3.5M use 12,800 and 25,600 items and are run for MemAgent only
no separate limit: the memory is the whole update output, capped by max_tokens=1,024, so an overlong memory is cut mid-sentence (App. F.1 shows this)

paper_vs_code.paper: stage II trains on inputs up to 60K tokens
paper_vs_code.code: the released 14B script trains on the 32K set with the default max_chunks=8, so contexts over 40K tokens would be centre-truncated; no stage II script is released

open_questions: Baselines read at most 120K tokens (990K for the 1M models), with the middle cut out, so beyond those lengths the comparison is between reading everything and reading a truncated input.
No run separates the RL-learned write policy from the chunked workflow at matched length except the w/o-RL rows; the no-RL agent is the untrained instruct model, not a prompted strong model.

key_numbers.label: Training data
key_numbers.value: stage I 32,768 × ~32K tokens; stage II 2,560 up to 60K

discussion.takeaway: A fixed-size, overwritten text memory trained with RL on the final answer lets a model with an 8K window handle inputs of millions of tokens with a small drop, where long-context models collapse past their windows.

claims.claim: Near-lossless extrapolation far beyond the training length.
claims.evidence: RL-MemAgent-14B 80.47 at 7K and 71.09 at 3.5M on RULER-HQA; 7B 81.25 → 71.88. Table 1
Qwen2.5-Instruct-14B-1M 60.16 at 7K, 0.00 at 896K; QwenLong-L1-32B 11.72 at 896K. Table 1

claims.claim: RL is what makes the workflow work.
claims.evidence: NIAH avg at 512K: 14B w/o RL 40.10 vs RL 98.18. Fig. 5; RULER-HQA and LongBench-QA plots, Fig. 6-7

claims.claim: The learned memory transfers to other tasks.
claims.evidence: LongBench-QA avg 51.0 (14B) vs 50.7 QwenLong-L1-32B, Table 3; best or second-best ROUGE recall on GovReport and QMSum, Table 2

claims.claim: Better than RAG over the same text.
claims.evidence: RULER-HQA at 3.5M: best RAG row 66.41 (Qwen2.5-14B, K=6) vs 71.09; LongBench-QA avg: best RAG 39.42 (14B, 2,048-token chunks, K=8) vs 51.00. Tables 10-11

claims.claim: The 1,024-token memory is a reasonable choice and results are stable across 256-4,096.

limits: No limitations section. The authors show failure cases: early distractors fill the memory and a key fact appended later is cut off; a multi-hop fact seen before its bridge is not kept; an early wrong reading of the question is reinforced (App. F).
reading: RULER-HQA is built the same way as the stage I training data (§3.1), so Table 1 is in-distribution in task type; only the length is out of distribution.
Baselines are run with 120K inputs (990K for the 1M models) and the code cuts the middle of longer inputs, so above those lengths they see only part of the document while MemAgent reads all of it.

Answers are sampled at temperature 0.7 with one sample per question in the released evaluation, and RULER-HQA has 128 questions per length, so differences of a few points are within one or two questions' worth of noise (1 question = 0.78 points).
Mem0 is described as a baseline in App. D.2 (GPT-5.1, top-30 memories) but no Mem0 number appears in any table or figure.
The LongBench-QA gain over the 32B reasoning baselines is small (51.0 vs 50.7 and 49.0 avg), and on NarrativeQA and Qasper MemAgent-14B is within 1-2 points of them.

abstract.text: MemAgent turns long-document question answering into a loop: the model reads the text in fixed chunks and after each one rewrites a short memory, then answers from that memory alone. Because the memory has a fixed size, cost grows linearly with length and the model's own window never has to grow. The authors train the memory updates with an extension of DAPO in which every update call shares the reward of the final answer. Models trained on 32K-60K inputs with an 8K window keep most of their accuracy up to 3.5M tokens and score above 95% on 512K needle tests.
